themes.theme: Reverse DCF confidence in conservative growth estimates
Quality companies vs. deep value timing

positions.commentary: The speaker discusses the uncertainty around Meta's growth returning to 20% due to ATT deprecating targeting, but suggests a 3-5% growth assumption might be acceptable if AI spending signals are positive.
The speaker suggests that Copart will provide a return that is a fair assumption for an investor comfortable owning an above average company.

thesis: The episode argues that investors should prioritize confidence in conservative growth estimates (e.g., 3% for Meta) over high-growth assumptions, noting that Meta's recent performance validates higher bands even if not required for a bullish decision. It further suggests that high-quality companies with strong moats, such as Copart, are better suited for growth investors who accept fair returns rather than deep value investors waiting for rare cheap entry points.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests it is easier to have confidence in a conservative growth estimate for Meta (at least 3%) rather than a high one (20%+), implying a comfortable lower bound.
claims.quote: And so, again, the idea there is that it would be much easier to have confidence that meta is going to grow at least 3%, then say, oh, I think they're going to return to, you know, you know, 20% plus growth, have margin expansion.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Meta returned to 20% plus growth and margin expansion, validating the high band of outcomes despite not needing confidence in it for the decision.
claims.quote: And of course, that is what happened. But you didn't need to have confidence in this kind of high band of outcomes in order to make a decision at that time.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that the memo used a snapshot of inputs and reverse DCF outputs for Meta as a good example, noting the date was October 15th, 2024.
claims.quote: And yeah, I loved, I loved in this memo how you kind of took exactly the snapshot of the inputs and the reverse DCF outputs of meta. And, you know, of course, it was a, it was a good example to use because as of October or 15th, 2024, you know, you look pretty smart, I have to say.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Meta as a company that went from growing 20% year over year for every year they've been public, before material changes to the business.
claims.quote: Again, you had a company that went from growing, you know, year over year, 20% for every year they've been public. Then obviously, there were some material changes to the business, but the beauty of the versus you have to show the assumptions that you needed to be made.

claims.claim: The speaker discusses the uncertainty around Meta's growth returning to 20% due to ATT deprecating targeting, but suggests a 3-5% growth assumption might be acceptable if AI spending signals are positive.
claims.quote: But again, it was kind of like, okay, well, maybe I'm not sure they're going to get back to 20% growth, but if I think that, you know, they're spending all this money on AI and maybe Mark Zuckerberg knows what he's doing, and maybe they have some signal back, am I okay with a three to five percent?

claims.claim: The speaker states that one cannot expect to buy a company with very strong moats and good prospects like Copart and assume a 15% return with very reasonable assumptions.
claims.quote: You should not expect that just because you want a 15% return. You're going to be able to buy a company with very with very strong modes, very good prospects like Copart with that sort of assumed return and very reasonable assumptions. That won't necessarily happen.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that owning Copart is a fair assumption for a real growth investor or quality guy, noting it provides a likely return.
claims.quote: But it's almost when you see the reverse DCF output that Speedwell puts out on the reports. You almost can see, oh, this is what, like, a real growth investor would assume. This is kind of like what a quality guy would assume. This is kind of what, like, a deep value investor would assume where, like, they wouldn't invest if they have to make any Herculean assumptions.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that a deep value investor might miss opportunities because they wait for a high quality company like Copart to get cheap, which rarely happens.
claims.quote: And you kind of see how these guys all think, right? You're kind of like, oh, how like a deep value investor probably missed it 95% of the opportunities because they wait for a company get to a price so cheap that more likely or not, that's not going to happen unless you're in a, you know, very rare instances in humanity is a great quality company is going to get that cheap, right?

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that Copart will provide a return that is a fair assumption for an investor comfortable owning an above average company.
claims.quote: Either you have to kind of go along with that and just say, hey, look, I'm comfortable owning a above average company and, you know, maybe I don't know what the SMP is going to do over the next 10 years, but I'm confident. Co-part's going to, you know, provide more likely or not this return, then, you know, that's a fair assumption.
